--
[happy to hang around for the time zones, and NOT just listening in for the accent nostalgia ~wink~]
H/T @duane Wilkins | Toitū Te Whenua Land Information New Zealand
“Research reports and historical records contain thousands of references to pā, kāinga, marae, awa, maunga, ara and other places. These names connect whenua with people, journeys, events and whakapapa, but they can be hard to find across hundreds of pages.
In this practical online wānanga, you’ll learn how to use AI locally on your desktop computer to search large PDFs while keeping the working files on your computer. We will find possible place names and the kōrero around them, keep each result connected to its original source, then view the reviewed results on a map.
We will finish by creating a simple place-to-place journey in Google Earth 3D. No AI, data or GIS experience is needed. If you can open a PDF and use a web browser, you can follow the demonstration…
     • Ngā puna raraunga | DATA SOURCES USED IN THE DEMONSTRATION
            - Waitangi Tribunal research reports and inquiry documents
            - The New Zealand Gazetteer of official and recorded place names
            - New Zealand Gazette notices and published Treaty settlement place-name records.
     • He mea nui mō tātou | WHY THIS MATTERS
            - Māori data is a taonga. Place names and place-based kōrero need care, appropriate access and protection
            - A local-first approach can support rangatiratanga and greater mana whakahaere by keeping approved files and draft results under your control
            - Keeping the whakapapa of the data visible makes every result easier for whānau, hapū, iwi, researchers and mana whenua to review
            - The purpose is collective benefit, helping whanau reconnect information with identity, place, te reo and future aspirations.
     • Ko wai mā tēnei | WHO THIS IS FOR
            - Iwi, hapū, marae and Māori land trusts working with whenua, history, records or taonga information.
            - Kaitiaki, whānau researchers, historians, planners, archivists and people preparing material for hui
            - Anyone curious about using local AI to explore place-based kōrero and create a map
            - Beginners are welcome. No AI, data, mapping or GIS experience is needed…”
